title: Choosing Manual Therapy and the Maitland Concept
lead: How to choose a technique, how to dose it, and how to know if it worked.

sections.title: 13.1 What manual therapy can and cannot do

blocks.text: Manual therapy (mobilisation, manipulation, soft-tissue techniques) can reduce pain and improve movement in the short term, mainly through neurophysiological effects (changes in pain processing and muscle activity) [Ref – to verify]. It does not "put bones back in place" or permanently change tissue structure. Its best use is to create a window of reduced pain and better movement, which you then use for exercise and function.

blocks.label: TEACHER'S VOICE
body: Manual therapy opens the door. Exercise walks through it.

sections.title: 13.2 Safety screen before any manual therapy

rows: Precautions (modify technique, reduce force, seek advice)
Suspected fracture, instability, malignancy at the site, infection
Cauda equina or cord compression signs
Vascular signs (cervical artery dysfunction, Vol 2 Ch 6)
Acute inflammatory arthritis at the target joint
Severe pain or high irritability, neurological signs

sections.title: 13.3 Selecting a technique: a decision sequence

items: **Identify the comparable sign** (the movement or test reproducing the patient's symptom).
**Match technique to findings**: stiffness with pain at end range suggests mobilisation at end range; pain before resistance suggests gentle low-grade mobilisation.
**Apply and re-test** the comparable sign immediately.
**Decide**: improvement continues the technique; no change after 2 to 3 attempts changes the technique; worsening stops it.

blocks.text: Geoffrey Maitland's approach uses careful clinical reasoning, detailed examination of movement and passive accessory movements, and graded oscillatory mobilisation. The "brick wall" concept separates theoretical knowledge (diagnosis) from clinical presentation (signs and symptoms), so treatment can be guided by what the patient shows even when the exact structure is unknown.

rows: Small amplitude at the beginning of range
Large amplitude within range, not reaching resistance
Small amplitude into resistance at end range
Central PA (posterior-anterior) pressure, lumbar or thoracic
Pisiform or thumbs over the spinous process; oscillate downward through straight arms using body weight
Thumbs over the articular pillar or transverse process on one side
Stabilise the scapula; web space on the proximal humerus; glide downward (for elevation stiffness)
Stabilise the femur; glide the tibia backward (for flexion)
Stabilise the tibia; glide the talus backward (for dorsiflexion)

items: Typical treatment bouts of about 30 to 60 seconds, repeated 2 to 4 times, then re-assess [Ref – to verify]. Low irritability: higher grades, more repetitions.
High irritability: grades I to II, fewer repetitions, stop at first sign of increased symptoms.
**What is the main mechanism of manual therapy?** Neurophysiological effects on pain and muscle activity, not structural repositioning.
**Which grade for a stiff but not irritable knee?** Grade III to IV.
**What do you do after 2 to 3 bouts without change?** Change the technique or approach.
**Name two absolute contraindications.** Suspected fracture and cauda equina signs (also malignancy, infection, vascular signs).
**Why re-test immediately?** To know whether the technique changed the comparable sign.

sections.title: Now You Should Be Able To

items: Choose and dose Maitland grades by irritability.
Use the comparable sign to judge effect.
